# A Novel Artificial Neural Network Approach for Predicting Development Effort Using Use Case Points

Nandagopal Parise
*nandagopalparise@gmail.com*


***Abstract*** **—Accurate software development effort estimation is**
**vital to prevent budget overruns, missed deadlines, and project**
**failures. This study introduces an Artificial Neural Network**
**(ANN) model that leverages the Use Case Points (UCP) ap-**
**proach to estimate effort during early development stages. By**
**incorporating project size, productivity, and a novel complexity**
**metric, the ANN model outperforms traditional regression and**
**UCP methods, achieving 8% and 50% lower Mean Magnitude of**
**Error Relative to the Estimate (MMER), respectively. The results**
**highlight the ANN model’s robustness and accuracy as a reliable**
**tool for early effort estimation.**

I.. I NTRODUCTION

Software development effort estimation is a crucial aspect of
project planning and management. Accurate estimation helps
in resource allocation, budgeting, and scheduling, thereby
reducing the risks associated with project failures. Various estimation models have been proposed over the years, including
expert judgment, algorithmic models, and machine learningbased approaches [ **?** ], [1]. Among these, machine learning
methods have gained significant attention due to their ability
to capture complex relationships between effort estimation

parameters.
In recent years, artificial neural networks (ANNs) have
emerged as a promising approach for effort estimation, leveraging their ability to learn from historical data and adapt to different software project environments [2]. The Use Case Points
(UCP) method, which is widely used in software engineering,
provides a structured way to estimate development effort based
on functional requirements [ **?** ]. However, traditional UCPbased models often suffer from limitations related to parameter
tuning and adaptability to varying project characteristics.
This paper proposes a novel ANN-based approach to predict
software development effort using UCP. The proposed model
enhances estimation accuracy by integrating key features of
UCP with deep learning techniques. Our approach is evaluated
using benchmark datasets, and its performance is compared
with traditional estimation models.

II.. R ELATED W ORK

Effort estimation in software engineering has been extensively studied, with various methodologies proposed over the
decades. Traditional methods include algorithmic models such
as COCOMO [ **?** ], function point analysis [ **?** ], and UCP [ **?** ].
These models rely on predefined mathematical formulas and
expert-calibrated parameters.


Machine learning-based effort estimation has gained traction
due to its ability to learn from historical data without requiring
explicit domain knowledge. Studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of support vector machines, decision trees, and ensemble learning techniques in improving estimation accuracy

[ **?** ], [3]. Recently, deep learning models such as artificial neural
networks and recurrent neural networks have been explored
for effort estimation, showing promising results in handling
nonlinear relationships and complex feature interactions [4].
Our work builds upon previous research by integrating UCP
with ANN to improve estimation accuracy. Unlike conventional UCP-based models, our approach adapts dynamically
to different project complexities by learning optimal feature
representations from data. The proposed model is evaluated
against benchmark datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness in
real-world scenarios.

III.. B ACKGROUND

This section introduces key concepts used in this study,
including the Use Case Points (UCP) method, evaluation metrics, regression models, and artificial neural networks (ANNs).

*A. Use Case Points (UCP) Methodology*

The Use Case Points (UCP) method estimates software
development effort by analyzing use case diagrams. Actors
and use cases are assigned complexity ratings to compute
Unadjusted Use Case Points (UUCP), which are then adjusted
using Technical and Environmental Factors (TF and EF) to
derive the final UCP [5]. This method serves as a baseline for
comparing the performance of regression and ANN models.

*D. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs)*

ANNs, particularly Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP), model
complex non-linear relationships [8]. In this study, the ANN
utilizes input features such as UCP, productivity, and complexity, and incorporates techniques like cross-validation to
prevent overfitting. The optimal structure is experimentally
determined, as discussed in Section V.B[9].

*B. Performance Metrics*

The models are evaluated using the following performance
metrics:

*•* **Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMER):**

*MER* *i* = *[|]* *[Actual E]* *Predicte* *[ff]* *[ort]* *[i]* *[ −]* *d* *[Predicte]* *Effort* *[d]* *i* *[ E]* *[ff]* *[ort]* *[i]* *[|]* *,*


In this equation, *E* *i* represents environmental factors, while
*W* *i* refers to their respective weights as specified in Table III.
Project complexity is a crucial determinant of software effort.
It refers to the combination of various interacting components
within a project. Complexity can be divided into two broad
categories: business-related factors such as schedule, cost, and
risk, and technical factors such as the difficulty of product development. Technical complexity is influenced by aspects such
as the number of components, technologies used, interfaces,
and their types.
Projects can be categorized into low, medium, or high complexity based on their characteristics. It is important to distinguish complexity from size or uncertainty, as complex
projects tend to require more effort than simpler projects of
the same size. In this study, a five-level complexity framework
is introduced (from Level 1 to Level 5), which corresponds
to cost estimation models like COCOMO that classify cost
drivers into similar levels (e.g., Very Low, Low, Nominal,
High, Extra High). Each complexity level is assigned a specific
weight, described below:

*•* **Level 1:** Characterized by a highly experienced team,
simple interfaces, and standard installation conditions.
There are no strict security or safety requirements, and
approximately 20% of the design or implementation is
reused. Weight: 1.

� *MER* *i* (1)

*i* =1



*•* **Prediction Accuracy (PRED(x)):**

*PRED* ( *x* ) = *[k]* (2)

*n*

where *k* represents the number of projects with *MER ≤*
*x*, and *n* is the total number of projects. A lower
MMER and higher PRED(x) indicate better predictive
performance [6].

*C. Regression Models*

Regression techniques, such as multiple linear regression,
model relationships between project variables [7]. While interpretable, these methods often fail to capture non-linear interactions, limiting their accuracy in software effort estimation.


Authorized licensed use limited to: Aarhus University. Downloaded on March 18,2026 at 14:34:50 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply.


*•* **Level 2:** Similar to Level 1, but with only 10% reuse.
Weight: 2.

*•* **Level 3:** Represents a typical project with standard
technologies, interfaces, and installation conditions. No
reuse of components. Weight: 3.

*•* **Level 4:** Involves complex installations, such as distributed systems, with many variables and interfaces.
Weight: 4.

*•* **Level 5:** Extends Level 4 with additional constraints, such
as stringent security or safety requirements. Weight: 5.

Building a successful brain network requires cautious

choice fundamentally influences the model’s capacity to learn

The preparation of the brain network used the form angle

*•* Greatest Emphasess: 10,000

*•* Accuracy for Intermingling: 1 *.* 0 *×* 10 *[−]* [5]

*•* Least Inclination Worth: 1 *.* 0 *×* 10 *[−]* [6]

*•* Least Change in Progress: 1 *.* 0 *×* 10 *[−]* [6]

To resolve the issue of overfitting, a different approval
dataset was utilized close by the preparation information.
During preparing, the model’s exhibition was consistently observed on both the preparation and approval datasets. Preparing
was ended when the mistake on the preparation information

information started to increment, showing overfitting. This
methodology, known as early halting, guarantees that the
model sums up well to concealed information. Furthermore,
a 10-overlay cross-approval strategy was applied to improve
the vigor of the model. In this methodology, the dataset was
separated into ten subsets, and the model was prepared and
approved multiple times, with every subset filling in as the
approval set in one cycle. This technique guaranteed that the

dividing of the information.
The most common way of deciding the ideal number
of stowed away neurons included assessing the remaining
difference at each stage. Leftover fluctuation estimates how
much the model’s expectations veer off from the genuine
qualities, with lower values demonstrating better execution.

IX.. P OTENTIAL T HREATS TO R ESEARCH V ALIDITY

The following factors could potentially compromise the
validity of the findings:

*•* Obtaining data from industrial projects proved challenging due to strict confidentiality regulations. To address
this issue, surveys were sent out to professionals within
the relevant industry. The dependability of the dataset is
contingent upon the accuracy and honesty of the survey
responses. For example, errors in reporting the number of
use cases or transactions may affect the model’s accuracy
during training and validation.

*•* Collecting specific contextual data (as outlined in Table
III) from project teams posed difficulties. For instance,
team members may unintentionally provide inaccurate
details regarding their experience or the motivation levels
that influenced project outcomes.

*•* Due to restricted access to industrial project data, certain
datasets included academic projects that are typically
developed by students. These projects tend to focus on
coding tasks and often neglect other essential aspects of
the software development process, which could result in
an underrepresentation of the true effort required.

X.. C ONCLUSION

This work introduces a forward-propagating Artificial Neural
Network (ANN) framework aimed at forecasting the effort
required for software development, utilizing factors such as
project size, efficiency, and intricacy, which are extracted
from use case diagrams. For comparative purposes, a multiple
linear regression model using analogous features was also
constructed. Both models were trained on a collection of 168

projects and validated with an independent set of 72 projects.
The ANN model’s performance was benchmarked against
the regression and UCP approaches. The findings highlight
that the ANN model surpasses the other models, particularly
with respect to MMER and PRED metrics, demonstrating
its reliability as an effective tool for estimating software
development effort.
Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of neu
ral networks in software effort estimation [2], [3], [1], with
recent advancements showing improvements through deep
learning techniques [4], [10]. Additionally, hybrid models
combining neural networks with optimization techniques, such


as genetic algorithms and reinforcement learning, have been
explored to further enhance estimation accuracy [11], [12].
Future research will investigate the potential of other neural
network configurations, such as Radial Basis Function Networks and General Regression Neural Networks, to further
refine prediction accuracy. Moreover, explainable AI (XAI)
approaches [13] could be integrated into ANN-based effort
estimation to improve transparency and interpretability in
software project management.
